2. Review what changed. Look at the summary first, then the details:

git status
git diff

Use git diff --stat for a quick overview of which files changed and by how much.

3. Run the tests. Make sure the code compiles and the tests pass before committing. The agent said it works, but we should check.

4. Commit the finished work. Stage deliberately and write a clear message:

git add -p
git commit -m "Add input validation to the signup form"

git add -p lets us choose hunk by hunk, so unrelated edits do not slip into the commit.

Useful Habits

Start from a clean state. Before giving the agent a task, commit or stash our own work. Then git diff shows only the agent’s changes.

git status          # should be clean
git switch -c agent/fix-signup   # optional: a branch for the task

Keep tasks small. One task, one commit. A small task finishes quickly, and its diff is easy to review.

Undo safely. If the result is not what we wanted, a clean starting point makes discarding it easy. To drop the agent’s uncommitted changes to one file:

git restore path/to/file
Warning

git restore and git checkout -- <file> throw away uncommitted changes for good. Check git diff first.

Working in Parallel with a Worktree

Sometimes we want to keep working while the agent runs. The safe way is to give the agent its own copy of the repository using git worktree. Each worktree has its own working directory and branch, but they share one history, so neither of us disturbs the other’s files.

git worktree add ../myproject-agent -b agent/task
cd ../myproject-agent
# start the agent here, while we keep working in the original folder

When the agent is done, we review and commit in the worktree, then merge the branch as usual and clean up:

git worktree remove ../myproject-agent

Quick Summary

Situation What to do
Agent is still editing Don’t stage or commit; wait
Agent says it is done git status, git diff, run tests
Changes look good One clean commit with a clear message
Want to work at the same time Use a separate git worktree and branch
Result is wrong git restore the files, or discard the branch

item.title: Hex Color Codes Explained: How #FF8A3D Becomes a Colour
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
A hex color code is a six-character string used in web design (and in many other tools) to tell a screen how much red, green and blue (RGB) light to mix. It always starts with a hash sign, #.

Anatomy of a Hex Code

The six characters split into three pairs, and each pair controls one colour channel:

Pair Channel In #RRGGBB
First Red RRGGBB
Second Green RRGGBB
Third Blue RRGGBB

How the Base-16 System Works

Hexadecimal is a base-16 number system. Decimal counts 0 to 9 before rolling over; hexadecimal keeps going to 16 symbols by using the letters A to F for the values 10 to 15:

Hex digit 0–9 A B C D E F
Value 0–9 10 11 12 13 14 15

F is the largest value a single digit can have. A pair therefore runs from 00 (channel off, decimal 0) to FF (full intensity, decimal 255).

Converting a pair to 0–255

  1. Multiply the first character by 16.
  2. Multiply the second character by 1.
  3. Add the two results.

Example: FF. F is 15, so (15 × 16) + 15 = 240 + 15 = 255.

Example: A3. A is 10, so (10 × 16) + 3 = 160 + 3 = 163.

Now we can read the code from the figure, #FF8A3D:

Channel Pair Calculation Value
Red FF 15 × 16 + 15 255
Green 8A 8 × 16 + 10 138
Blue 3D 3 × 16 + 13 61

That is a strong red, a medium green and a little blue, which gives the orange in the figure.

Checking It in R

R programming language understands hex colours, so we can confirm the conversion with col2rgb():

col2rgb("#FF8A3D")
      [,1]
red    255
green  138
blue    61

And rgb() goes the other way, from numbers to a hex code:

rgb(255, 138, 61, maxColorValue = 255)
[1] "#FF8A3D"

Hex is only one way to write the same numbers. RGB Color Codes Explained covers the decimal form, rgb(255, 138, 61), and rgba() for transparency.

Common Examples

Colour Code Meaning
Pure red #FF0000 Max red, no green, no blue
Pure green #00FF00 No red, max green, no blue
Pure blue #0000FF No red, no green, max blue
White #FFFFFF All channels at maximum
Black #000000 All channels off
Grey #787878 Equal values in all three pairs

Any code whose three pairs are identical is a shade of grey. For #787878, each pair is 7 × 16 + 8 = 120.

Note

Hex codes follow an additive light model: higher values make a colour brighter and closer to white, not darker as with paint.

Handy Variations

  • Short form: when each pair has two identical digits, it can be shortened to three, so #FF0000 becomes #F00.
  • With transparency: an eight-character code adds a fourth pair for opacity, as in #FF8A3D80 (about 50%).

References

  2. How hex code colors work, freeCodeCamp
  3. Understanding hexadecimal colors, Pluralsight
  4. Hex colour codes explained, Corey Ginnivan
  5. ELI5: how hex code works, r/explainlikeimfive

item.title: Hybrid Stem-and-Leaf Plot: Stems of 5 for Finer Bins
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
A stem-and-leaf plot shows the shape of a dataset while keeping every original value. The usual version uses the tens digit as the stem, which can leave very few rows. Here is a simple fix: use stems that step by 5.

The Data

Here are 24 values:

13, 12, 6, 8, 15, 18, 17, 24, 28, 23, 27, 23,
21, 20, 15, 18, 23, 25, 23, 13, 17, 18, 19, 18

The Standard Plot: Only 3 Rows

With the tens digit as the stem and the units digit as the leaf, we get:

Stem | Leaf
  0  | 6 8
  1  | 2 3 3 5 5 7 7 8 8 8 8 9
  2  | 0 1 3 3 3 3 4 5 7 8

Key: 1 | 3 means 13

This gives only three classes, and most of the data sits in two of them. The shape is hard to see.

The Hybrid Plot: Stems of 5

If the stems are 5, 10, 15, 20 and 25, the data fall into bins of width 5. Each leaf is the value minus its stem:

Stem | Leaf
  5  | 1 3
 10  | 2 3 3
 15  | 0 0 2 2 3 3 3 3 4
 20  | 0 1 3 3 3 3 4
 25  | 0 2 3

Key: 15 | 3 means 15 + 3 = 18

For example, the stem 15 covers 15 to 19, so its leaves stand for 15, 15, 17, 17, 18, 18, 18, 18 and 19. We now see five bins instead of three, and the peak in the 15 to 19 range stands out.

Note

This is a hybrid between a stem-and-leaf plot and a histogram with bins of width 5. Unlike a histogram, it keeps the exact data values.

Why It Works

  1. More bins. Five rows show the shape of the distribution more clearly than three.
  2. Same as a split-stem plot. It is equivalent to the usual split-stem plot, which writes each stem twice (low half, high half). Here the stems are written as numbers (10, 15) instead of symbols (1*, 1.).
  3. A bridge to histograms. The rows are the bars of a histogram turned sideways, but every value is still readable.

The Catch

A standard plot needs no arithmetic: 1 | 4 is simply 14. With stems of 5 the reader has to add (15 + 3 = 18). A clear Key fixes this, so always include one.

Doing It in R

R’s stem() function draws this kind of plot. The scale argument controls how many rows we get. With scale = 0.5 we get the three-row plot:

x <- c(13, 12, 6, 8, 15, 18, 17, 24, 28, 23, 27, 23,
       21, 20, 15, 18, 23, 25, 23, 13, 17, 18, 19, 18)

stem(x, scale = 0.5)
  The decimal point is 1 digit(s) to the right of the |

  0 | 68
  1 | 233557788889
  2 | 0133334578

By default (scale = 1) R splits each stem in two, which is exactly the width-5 bins:

stem(x)
  The decimal point is 1 digit(s) to the right of the |

  0 | 68
  1 | 233
  1 | 557788889
  2 | 0133334
  2 | 578

Here the lower 1 row holds 12 to 14 and the upper 1 row holds 15 to 19. This layout avoids the arithmetic problem, because each leaf is simply the units digit.

Summary

If the data are tightly clustered and a standard stem-and-leaf plot gives too few rows, use stems of 5 (or R’s default split stems). We get more bins without losing the raw values. Just include a clear key.

item.title: The Monte Carlo Method Explained: Estimating π with Random Points
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
Some problems are too messy for a neat formula: the chance that a portfolio crashes, the path of a particle through a material, the best move in a board game. The Monte Carlo method solves them by brute-force randomness. We simulate the situation many times with random inputs, and read the answer off the results. Let’s see the idea on the simplest example, and then build it in R.

What Is the Monte Carlo Method?

A Monte Carlo method estimates a quantity by repeating a random experiment many times and averaging what happens. The name comes from the Monte Carlo casino in Monaco, a nod to the role of chance. The recipe has the same four steps every time:

  1. Define the range of possible inputs.
  2. Generate random inputs from it.
  3. Compute the result for each input (here, a simple yes/no).
  4. Combine the results, usually by averaging, into the estimate.

It works because of the law of large numbers: the more random samples we use, the closer their average gets to the true value. The error shrinks roughly like , so ten times the accuracy costs a hundred times the samples. This is slow, but it works for almost any problem, however complicated.

The Dirt-Throwing Analogy

Imagine a perfectly round circle drawn inside a square on a wall. We want the area of the circle, but we pretend we do not know its formula. So we play a game:

  1. Throw blindfolded. We throw 1,000 handfuls of dirt at the wall.
  2. One rule. Every throw must land somewhere inside the square.
  3. Count. We count how many splatters landed inside the circle, and how many landed outside.

If 785 of 1,000 splatters land inside the circle, the circle covers about 78.5% of the square. Since the square’s area is easy (width × height), the circle’s area is that area times 0.785.

  • With 10 throws the estimate is poor, because of pure luck.
  • With a million throws the splatters fill the shape evenly and the estimate is very accurate.

Estimating π

Take a square from to on both axes, with a circle of radius 1 inside it. The square has area and the circle has area . So the share of points inside the circle should be , which gives

A point is inside the circle when .

Throwing the points in R

library(tidyverse)

set.seed(2026)
n <- 2000

points <- tibble(
  x = runif(n, -1, 1),
  y = runif(n, -1, 1)
) %>%
  mutate(inside = x^2 + y^2 <= 1)

4 * mean(points$inside)
[1] 3.172

runif() draws uniform random numbers, and mean() of a logical column is the share of TRUE values, so 4 * mean(inside) is exactly the formula above. The true value is 3.1416.

Seeing the points

circle <- tibble(t = seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 300)) %>%
  mutate(x = cos(t), y = sin(t))

ggplot(points, aes(x, y, colour = inside)) +
  geom_point(size = 1) +
  geom_path(data = circle, aes(x, y), colour = "black", inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  coord_fixed() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "seagreen", "FALSE" = "tomato"),
                      labels = c("TRUE" = "Inside", "FALSE" = "Outside")) +
  labs(title = "2000 random points in the square", colour = NULL)

The green points inside the circle make up about of all points.

More Throws, Better Estimate

How many points do we need? Let’s keep a running estimate as the points arrive and plot it.

set.seed(2026)
N <- 100000

running <- tibble(
  n = 1:N,
  inside = runif(N, -1, 1)^2 + runif(N, -1, 1)^2 <= 1
) %>%
  mutate(estimate = 4 * cumsum(inside) / n)

ggplot(running, aes(n, estimate)) +
  geom_line(colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = pi, colour = "tomato", linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(title = "The estimate settles down as n grows",
       x = "Number of points (log scale)", y = "Estimate of π")

At the start the line jumps around, which is the “pure luck” of few throws. After a few thousand points it hugs the dashed line at . A table shows the same story:

running %>%
  filter(n %in% c(10, 100, 1000, 10000, 100000)) %>%
  transmute(n, estimate = round(estimate, 4), error = round(abs(estimate - pi), 4))
# A tibble: 5 × 3
       n estimate  error
   <int>    <dbl>  <dbl>
1     10     3.2  0.0584
2    100     3.12 0.0216
3   1000     3.16 0.0224
4  10000     3.16 0.02  
5 100000     3.15 0.0036

The error shrinks as grows, though not steadily: a lucky small sample can beat an unlucky larger one.

Tip

Run the code again with a different set.seed(). The numbers change, but the pattern (wild at first, then steady) does not. That is the Monte Carlo method at work.

Why This Matters in Real Life

Computers use this “dirt-throwing” logic to simulate millions of random scenarios in seconds. It is used when the problem is too complex for a straight formula:

  • Finance: throwing random market events at a portfolio to see how often it crashes.
  • Physics: simulating billions of random paths a particle might take.
  • Games: letting an AI play thousands of random futures in chess or Go to choose a move.
  • Statistics: approximating integrals, p-values and posterior distributions that have no closed form.

Estimating π is not a good use of Monte Carlo, since much better methods exist. We use it because we know the answer, which lets us watch the method work.
